Sunday night, hostel
Went home for the weekend. Mistake. Papa and Mummy didn't speak at lunch, then shouted about money at dinner. Manoj, fifteen, put his earphones in and stared at his plate.
Afterwards Mummy came to my room and cried about Papa for an hour. Then Papa caught me on the stairs: "You're old enough now. Tell her she's being unreasonable." I nearly did. For a second I wanted to pick a side just to make the noise stop.
I didn't. I said, "Papa, I love you both. I'm not going to carry messages. Please talk to someone, a counsellor, anyone." He looked hurt. So did I, probably.
I took Manoj for a walk to the chai stall and told him none of this is our fault, and that he can call me any night. On the bus back I felt guilty for leaving, and relieved too. Both.
— Hemant

qa.q: What did Papa ask Hemant to tell Mummy?
qa.a: That she was being unreasonable.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel on the bus back to the hostel?
qa.a: Guilty for leaving and relieved at the same time.

qa.q: How did Hemant avoid taking a side?
qa.a: By refusing to carry messages, telling Papa that Hemant loves them both, suggesting a counsellor, and reassuring Manoj that it isn't their fault.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj at home?
qa.a: Tense and lonely; he shuts out the fights with earphones and needs to hear that none of it is his fault.

grounding: Shows parents' fights landing on a young adult, who refuses to take a side, loves both and keeps a healthy distance while supporting a younger sibling.

Home in their village near Sangli for the summer, Jatin found everything as it always was. His mother, Chandrika, woke at five, milked the buffaloes, packed his tiffin though he wasn't going anywhere, and said almost nothing. When he talked about his hostel, she said, "Hmm," and went back to the sugarcane accounts.
For years he had told himself she didn't care. In the city he'd watched friends chat with their mothers on video calls and felt a dull ache.
On the third morning he got up at five too. He didn't ask. He picked up the second bucket and followed her to the shed. She glanced at him and, without a word, showed him how to sit so the buffalo wouldn't kick.
They milked side by side. On the walk back she said, "Your father was always slow at this. You're faster." It was the longest sentence she'd said all week.
That evening she made his favourite puran poli. Later he called Prof. Kulkarni, his mentor, and talked for an hour about his project. Both were good.

qa.q: What time did Chandrika wake up?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: How had Jatin felt about his mother's silence?
qa.a: Hurt and unloved, telling himself she didn't care and feeling a dull ache when friends chatted with their mothers.

qa.q: How did Jatin reach his mother?
qa.a: In her own language, by getting up at five and milking the buffaloes beside her, while also talking deeper things through with Prof. Kulkarni.

qa.q: How does Chandrika show that she noticed Jatin?
qa.a: By quietly teaching him, praising his speed, and cooking his favourite puran poli that evening.

grounding: Illustrates emotional distance from a parent who provides but rarely talks, and connecting through shared tasks and food while seeking a mentor too.

She's my little sister. When she failed her driving test, I booked the retest. When her landlord raised the rent, I called him. When she couldn't decide between two jobs, I picked one. Every time she panicked, I swooped in. And then I'd hang up furious, thinking, why can't she do anything herself?

In Vikas's village near Karnal, everyone knew the canal ran fast after the rains. So when his sister Vasudha came home at dusk with wet hair, and Maa asked where she'd been, Vasudha shot him a look: cover for me.
He said nothing, and Maa let it go. Later, on the roof, Vasudha whispered, "Thanks. And don't tell them about Gurmeet either."
"About Gurmeet I won't say a word. That's yours to tell," Vikas said. "But the canal? Veeru's cousin nearly drowned there last monsoon."
"We only went in up to our knees."
"Then promise me you'll stop until the water drops, or I'm telling Maa tonight. I'm not keeping quiet about something that could kill you."
She glared. He didn't look away.
"Fine," she said at last. "Not till Diwali."
"And if the others push you, call me. I'll come on the cycle." He went down and asked Maa if the rotis were ready, carrying one secret and not the other.

qa.a: Wet hair.

In their village outside Dharwad, Hemant had run the family's small grocery and looked after their parents for three years while his sister Bhavna studied in Bengaluru. He never complained. He just kept a list in his head: every doctor trip, every bill, every night Appa couldn't sleep.

Sahil, you say your professor tears your code apart? Let me, your Bhavna bua, tell you about Professor Iyer.
It was 1990. I was twenty, one of three girls in the electrical engineering batch at our college. Professor Iyer returned my first lab report with more red ink than blue. I was so scared of him that for a month I just sat at the back and nodded.
Then I tried the other foolish thing: flattery. I told him his lecture was "brilliant, sir". He looked at me over his glasses and said, "Then you'll have a question about it." I didn't. My face burned.
After that I did it properly. I read the chapter before class. I went to his office on Thursdays with two written questions, never more, and left within ten minutes. When he corrected me, I wrote it down instead of arguing.
By final year he let me assist in his lab. So go with questions, Sahil, not compliments, and don't waste his time.

passage:
Dr. Seema Rao had fifteen minutes between her 2 o'clock and 3 o'clock classes, and Manjula had run through the rain from the hostel to catch them. Her dissertation chapter was due tomorrow, and the professor's last comment had been one line in red: "Your argument hides behind other people's quotes."
For a week Manjula had avoided her corridor. It felt easier to rewrite blindly than to ask.
Now she stood at the door, dripping. "Ma'am, I have two questions. I'll be quick."
Dr. Rao glanced at the clock. "Go."
"When you said my argument hides, do you mean fewer quotes, or my own claim first?"
"Your own claim first. Then the quotes serve it."
"And the second section, is it off-topic?"
"Yes. Cut it."
Manjula didn't argue. She wrote both answers down and was gone by 2:52. That night she rewrote the opening in her own words. The next comment, a week later, was also in red: "Better. Now push further."

qa.q: How long did Dr. Rao have between classes?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: Why had Manjula avoided Dr. Rao's corridor for a week?
qa.a: She felt afraid and intimidated by the red comment, and rewriting blindly seemed easier than asking.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that respected the professor's time?
qa.a: She came with exactly two clear questions, accepted the correction without arguing, wrote it down, and left by 2:52.

qa.q: How might Dr. Rao see Manjula's visit?
qa.a: As serious and efficient; the later comment "Better. Now push further." shows she values the effort.

grounding: Illustrates respecting a challenging professor: overcoming fear of asking, bringing focused questions and accepting correction.
